Only the fiduciary-capacity title with the conservatee's own taxpayer number keeps ownership clear and accountable.

question: A conservatee receives SSI and lives in a home owned by his sister, who charges no rent and pays his utilities. The conservatee has accumulated savings of $1,650 in the conservatorship estate. The conservator is concerned about benefit impact. Which statement most accurately describes the SSI risk?
options: There is no SSI impact at all, since his savings sit under the $2,000 resource limit and he is charged no rent for the home
The free housing and utilities are In-Kind Support and Maintenance, which can cut SSI by up to a third under the Presumed Value rule
The free housing provided by a relative is fully exempt from SSI because it is plainly a family gift rather than countable income
explanation: Shelter provided by another person is treated as In-Kind Support and Maintenance (ISM); since September 30, 2024, only shelter counts, not food. Under the Presumed Maximum Value rule SSI can be reduced by up to one-third of the federal benefit rate plus $20 (about $351 per month in 2026). Being under the $2,000 resource limit does not address that income reduction, so the no-impact answer is wrong. Treating relative-provided housing as an exempt gift is also wrong, because ISM is explicitly counted.

question: Which statement best describes the standard governing professional fiduciary fees in a California conservatorship of the estate?
options: Fees are a fixed statutory percentage of the estate's gross value, applied identically for every conservator in every case
Fees must be 'just and reasonable,' approved by the court on a noticed petition and supported by time records
Fees may be set by a private written contract with the conservatee's family members, without any court review or involvement
explanation: California Probate Code applies a 'just and reasonable' standard to conservator compensation, with the court weighing time spent, complexity, results, the conservator's license, and the estate's size, and contemporaneous timekeeping is essential support. A fixed statutory percentage describes probate-estate commissions, not conservator fees, which are not a strict percentage. A private fee agreement with the family cannot replace court approval, because the conservatee — not the family — is the fiduciary's principal, so that option is wrong.

question: A 35-year-old conservatee with developmental disabilities receives a $200,000 personal-injury settlement. He currently receives SSI and Medi-Cal. The conservator wants to preserve those benefits. Which trust is the appropriate vehicle?
options: A revocable living trust naming the conservatee as both the grantor and the lifetime beneficiary of the settlement funds
A first-party special needs trust under 42 U.S.C. §1396p(d)(4)(A), funded with the settlement and a Medicaid payback clause
A third-party special needs trust funded directly with the conservatee's own personal-injury settlement proceeds money
explanation: Because the settlement belongs to the disabled individual himself, the correct vehicle is a first-party (d4A) special needs trust authorized by OBRA-93: established for someone under 65, irrevocable, for his sole benefit, and containing a Medicaid payback at death. A revocable trust is a countable resource and offers no benefits protection. A third-party SNT is the inferior choice here because, despite the right label, it cannot be funded with the beneficiary's own money — the source of the funds is what controls.

question: Which of the following best describes how a California ABLE account interacts with SSI eligibility for a qualifying disabled individual?
options: All ABLE account balances are fully exempt from SSI resource counting, no matter how large the account grows over time
The first $100,000 in an ABLE account is excluded for SSI; amounts above that count toward the $2,000 limit and suspend SSI
ABLE accounts are treated just like ordinary bank savings accounts and are fully countable as a resource for SSI purposes
explanation: ABLE accounts give people with disabilities a tax-advantaged savings vehicle: up to $100,000 is excluded from the SSI resource calculation, and balances above that suspend (not terminate) SSI while Medicaid continues, with annual contributions capped ($20,000 in 2026 plus possible ABLE-to-Work additions). Claiming every balance is exempt at any amount overstates the protection. Treating an ABLE account like an ordinary, fully countable savings account ignores its special exclusion entirely, so that option is wrong.

question: When the court appoints a conservator of the estate, the conservator generally must post a bond. What is the primary purpose of the bond, and how is the amount typically calculated?
options: It is a filing fee paid to the court, set at one percent of the estate's gross appraised value at appointment
It protects the conservatee and creditors from the conservator's malfeasance, based on personal property plus a year's income
It is a non-refundable sum paid personally by the conservator that is forfeited entirely regardless of the case outcome
explanation: A surety bond protects the conservatorship estate against breach of fiduciary duty, and the amount is generally set to cover personal property plus one year's anticipated income, sometimes with add-ons for expected sales or recoveries, while real property held in fee is typically excluded. It is not a fee paid to the court calculated as a flat percentage. It is also not a personal, forfeited payment by the conservator; the premium buys coverage and is an estate expense, so that option is wrong.

question: A conservatee who has been on Medicare Part A and B is discharged from a 35-day hospital stay to a skilled nursing facility (SNF) for rehabilitation following a hip fracture. The conservator wants to know what Medicare will cover. Which statement is correct?
options: Part A covers SNF care for an unlimited time, as long as the conservatee keeps showing measurable improvement in rehab
Part A covers up to 100 SNF days per benefit period (days 1-20 full, days 21-100 coinsurance) given a 3-day inpatient stay
Medicare covers no skilled nursing facility costs at all; only the state Medi-Cal program ever pays for any SNF care
explanation: Medicare Part A SNF benefits require a qualifying three-day inpatient hospital admission (observation status does not count) and entry to a certified SNF within 30 days; days 1-20 are fully covered, days 21-100 carry daily coinsurance, and after day 100 the beneficiary is fully responsible. Medicare never covers true long-term custodial care, which is where Medi-Cal matters. Saying Part A covers SNF indefinitely overstates the duration, and saying Medicare covers no SNF at all is too absolute.

question: Which of the following best describes the VA Aid and Attendance pension benefit for a wartime veteran (or surviving spouse) requiring custodial care?
options: A monthly cash benefit available to all veterans over the age of 65, regardless of their wartime service or financial need
An enhanced pension for low-income wartime veterans or surviving spouses needing daily-living help, with a look-back and net-worth limit
A reimbursement program that pays VA hospitals and clinics directly for care, so the veteran personally never receives any cash
explanation: VA Aid and Attendance is an enhanced pension added to the basic VA pension for wartime veterans or surviving spouses who need help with activities of daily living, are bedridden, are in a nursing home, or have very limited eyesight; since October 2018 it carries a 36-month asset-transfer look-back and a published net-worth limit, and it is paid as monthly cash. Describing it as available to all veterans over 65 omits the wartime, ADL, and means-test requirements. It is not VA medical-care reimbursement, so that option confuses two programs.

question: Preparing the first accounting for the court, the conservator must classify several items. Which classification is most consistent with traditional fiduciary accounting principles?
options: Proceeds from the sale of a rental property are classified as 'income' simply because the cash was received during this accounting period
Rent and interest are 'income'; sale proceeds from estate assets are 'principal,' and capital improvements are charged to principal
Property taxes and ordinary routine maintenance costs on a rental property are charged against the estate's principal as capital
explanation: Fiduciary accounting distinguishes principal from income: receipts that replace the corpus, like sale proceeds, are principal, while receipts produced by the corpus, like rent and interest, are income, and extraordinary costs such as capital improvements are charged to principal. Calling sale proceeds 'income' simply because cash arrived this period misclassifies a principal receipt. Charging routine maintenance and property taxes against principal is also wrong, since those ordinary costs of producing income are typically charged to income.

question: A conservator pays an independent contractor (a handyman) $2,500 to repair fencing at the conservatee's rental property in 2026. Which statement about 1099 reporting is most accurate?
options: The payment topped the $2,000 threshold for a service to an unincorporated worker in a rental operation, so a 1099-NEC must issue
1099 reporting does not apply to conservatorships at all, because the conservatee herself is an individual and is not a business
Form 1099-NEC is required only when the total annual payments made to a single contractor exceed the $20,000 reporting threshold
explanation: Because the conservator operates rental real estate (treated as a trade or business) and paid $2,000 or more in the year (the threshold raised from $600 effective for payments after December 31, 2025) to a non-corporate service provider, Form 1099-NEC generally must issue by January 31 of the next year. Saying reporting never applies is wrong, since the conservator stands in the conservatee's shoes for the rental. The $20,000 figure confuses 1099-NEC with the separate 1099-K threshold for third-party network payments.

question: A conservatee created a fully funded revocable living trust years before her capacity declined. The trust names her as both grantor and lifetime beneficiary and names her son as successor trustee, effective on her incapacity. Now that conservatorship has been imposed, what is the conservator's relationship to the trust?
options: The conservatorship automatically dissolves the revocable trust, and the conservator then takes possession of all of the trust assets
The trust continues under its own terms with the successor trustee, while the conservator manages outside assets and coordinates
The conservator becomes the trustee by operation of law and replaces the son, the successor trustee named in the trust document
explanation: A funded revocable trust keeps operating during incapacity under its own succession rules — a core reason people create them. The successor trustee owes fiduciary duties to the conservatee as lifetime beneficiary, the conservator manages whatever assets sit outside the trust, and the two must coordinate. The conservatorship does not dissolve the trust, so the dissolution answer is wrong. The conservator also does not automatically replace the named successor trustee, which makes that option the inferior choice.

question: While marshaling a new conservatee's estate, the conservator suspects she has unclaimed property such as old bank accounts and uncashed dividend checks. Where is the best place to search?
options: Only the conservatee's single most recent federal and state income tax return from last year
The California State Controller's Unclaimed Property database, plus similar databases in other states where she has lived
Local newspaper classified advertisements and posted public notices in the conservatee's current neighborhood
explanation: The California State Controller maintains an Unclaimed Property database holding billions of dollars in dormant accounts, uncashed checks, safe-deposit contents, and abandoned securities, and searching every state where the conservatee lived is part of due diligence in marshaling assets. The most recent tax return is a useful starting point but misses assets that generate no recent income, so it is the inferior option. Local classified ads are not a recognized method for locating unclaimed property.

question: What is the role of the probate referee on the Inventory and Appraisal (Form DE-160/DE-161) filed in a California conservatorship?
options: To appraise the estate's non-cash assets at fair market value as of the appointment date
To audit the conservator's monthly bank account statements for the entire estate
To represent and advocate for the conservatee in person at all court hearings
explanation: California probate referees are court-appointed appraisers who value non-cash assets — real property, securities, businesses, personal property — at fair market value as of the conservator's appointment date, listing them on the referee's attachment to the inventory, while the conservator lists cash items separately. Monthly auditing of bank statements is part of the court's monitoring role, not the referee's. Representing the conservatee at hearings is the job of the conservatee's counsel or guardian ad litem, not the appraiser.

question: A conservatee owns a long-term care insurance policy paid up years ago. She has just been admitted to a memory-care assisted living facility costing $9,500 per month. The conservator should:
options: Wait to file a claim until she has paid privately for a full year, since long-term care insurance never pays out in the first year
Review the policy's triggering conditions and elimination period, gather medical records, and file a claim, self-paying during the wait
Cancel the long-term care insurance policy now to cut the monthly premium expense, since her memory-care stay has already begun
explanation: Most LTCi policies are triggered by inability to perform a set number of activities of daily living (often 2 of 6) or by severe cognitive impairment, and dementia in memory care typically qualifies; after a contractual elimination period of self-pay, benefits begin, and modern policies usually cover assisted living, not just nursing homes. Waiting a year to file is wrong because no such one-year rule exists. Canceling the policy wastes a paid-up asset just when its benefits are about to apply, making it the inferior choice.

question: A 68-year-old disabled conservatee on Medi-Cal receives a $40,000 inheritance. The conservator wants to preserve benefits but the conservatee is over 65 (disqualifying her from a standard first-party d4A trust in many cases). What option should the conservator most carefully evaluate?
options: Deposit the full inheritance into a new ABLE account to keep it from counting against Medi-Cal.
Contribute the funds to a nonprofit-managed pooled (d4C) special needs trust, which may accept beneficiaries of any age.
Spend the $40,000 down on her care needs over the coming month to restore her eligibility.
explanation: Pooled (d4C) special needs trusts, run by nonprofits with a separate sub-account per beneficiary, can accept first-party funding from individuals of any age, making them an important benefit-preservation tool for an over-65 disabled conservatee for whom a standard d4A trust is unavailable. An ABLE account cannot do the job here: ABLE eligibility requires disability onset before age 46, and the $40,000 inheritance far exceeds the annual ABLE contribution limit, so it cannot shelter these funds even if she qualified. A rushed spend-down is real planning in some cases but ignores documentation and prudent-management duties and can trigger transfer penalties if it is not a legitimate spend-down on her own needs; it also wastes funds that the pooled trust could preserve for her supplemental benefit.

question: A conservatee's estate includes a vacant single-family home in another state that has been empty for two years, generates no income, costs $14,000/year in taxes and insurance, and the conservatee has no plans to occupy it. Closest relatives have no interest in it. Under the prudent investor rule, what is the conservator's most defensible course of action?
options: Hold the property indefinitely, since real estate appreciates and hedges the estate against inflation.
Quitclaim the property to the closest relative for no consideration to shed the carrying cost.
Document the costs and lack of utility, weigh rent versus sale, appraise, and petition for court confirmation of sale.
explanation: The prudent investor rule requires evaluating each asset in the context of the whole portfolio and the conservatee's needs; a non-producing asset bleeding $14,000 a year with no future utility fails basic risk-adjusted-return principles. The conservator should analyze rent versus sale, obtain valuation, and follow the formal court-confirmation process for real property (notice, hearing, possible overbid). Simply holding the property treats real estate as automatically prudent and defends a wasting asset against the conservatee's interests. Quitclaiming it away for no consideration is a prohibited gift of estate assets and breaches the duty to preserve value, not a legitimate cost-saving move.

question: Assume a court has granted a substituted-judgment order allowing the conservator to make a $50,000 gift from the conservatee's estate to a charity and a $30,000 gift to each of two grandchildren in 2026. With respect to federal gift-tax reporting, which statement is most accurate?
options: No return is required, because a fiduciary acting for a conservatee is exempt from gift-tax filing rules.
File Form 709 for the grandchildren gifts above the exclusion; the charitable gift is generally deductible.
File a Form 706 estate tax return during her lifetime for any gift to a person exceeding the $1,000 limit.
explanation: Gifts made on behalf of a conservatee follow the same federal gift-tax rules as any individual. In 2026 the annual exclusion is about $19,000 per donee, so the $30,000 gifts to each grandchild require a Form 709, though the excess typically just reduces the lifetime unified credit rather than producing current tax. The charitable gift gets an unlimited charitable deduction and is generally not taxable, but may still be reported when other reportable gifts exist. There is no fiduciary exemption from gift-tax reporting, and the estate tax return (Form 706) is a death-time filing, not a lifetime gift form keyed to a $1,000 threshold.

question: On taking over a new conservatorship, the conservator reviews existing insurance and finds: a homeowner's policy with $250,000 dwelling coverage on a home now worth $1.1 million; auto insurance on a vehicle the conservatee can no longer drive; no umbrella policy; and a small whole-life policy with cash value. What is the most prudent action plan?
options: Cancel every existing policy and self-insure the property and liability exposures from estate funds.
Raise dwelling coverage to rebuilding cost, reassess the unused auto policy, and review umbrella and life options.
Leave each coverage exactly as found so the conservatee's existing arrangements stay undisturbed.
explanation: A conservator of the estate must protect assets, which includes maintaining adequate insurance. The $250,000 dwelling limit on a $1.1 million home exposes the estate to catastrophic under-insurance, so coverage should be raised to current rebuilding cost. The auto policy on a car the conservatee cannot drive should be evaluated (non-renew, or convert to comprehensive/garaged if a caregiver uses it), umbrella liability is cheap protection against major exposures, and the cash-value policy should be analyzed for continue, reduce-to-paid-up, or surrender. Canceling everything to self-insure is reckless, and leaving all coverage untouched abdicates the protection duty in the face of obvious gaps.

question: A conservatee on Medi-Cal long-term care dies owning her home (titled solely in her name) and a brokerage account. Her adult son, who lived with and cared for her in the home for the last 4 years before her institutionalization, hopes to inherit the house. What is the most accurate statement about Medi-Cal estate recovery in California today?
options: California recovers from all assets, including living-trust property and beneficiary-designated accounts, regardless of probate.
Since the 2017 reforms recovery is generally limited to probate assets, and the caregiver-child exemption may protect the home.
Recovery reaches only the assets she acquired after she first began receiving Medi-Cal benefits.
explanation: California significantly narrowed Medi-Cal estate recovery effective January 1, 2017. Recovery now generally targets only probate-estate assets, so property passing outside probate (revocable living trusts, joint tenancy, transfer-on-death deeds, beneficiary-designated accounts) is generally exempt. Hardship waivers and the caregiver-child exemption (a child who lived in the home and provided care that delayed institutionalization for at least two years) can further protect the house. The view that California reaches every asset regardless of probate reflects the overbroad pre-2017 rule, and there is no rule limiting recovery to assets acquired after benefits began.

question: Which California state agency licenses and regulates Residential Care Facilities for the Elderly (RCFEs), commonly known as assisted living facilities?
options: California Department of Social Services (CDSS), Community Care Licensing Division
California Department of Public Health (CDPH), which oversees licensed health facilities
California Department of Aging, which administers the long-term care ombudsman program
explanation: RCFEs (assisted living) are licensed by the California Department of Social Services, Community Care Licensing Division. CDPH licenses skilled nursing facilities and other medical facilities, so it is the wrong regulator for non-medical assisted living. The Department of Aging administers the long-term care ombudsman program but does not license facilities at all. A conservator placing a conservatee must verify licensing status with the correct regulator, which makes the distinction practical, not academic.

question: A newly appointed conservator must decide on housing for an 82-year-old conservatee with moderate dementia who has been living alone with a daily home health aide. The conservatee wanders occasionally but has not left the property. The family is pushing for immediate placement in a locked memory care unit. What is the conservator's best first step?
options: Place the conservatee in the memory care unit now, since the whole family clearly supports that move
Assess functioning, weigh whether enhanced in-home supports could safely maintain his current placement
Petition the court right away for authority to place him in a locked secured-perimeter dementia facility
explanation: The conservator must choose the most appropriate, least-restrictive setting. Before a locked facility, that means assessing current functioning, evaluating whether enhanced in-home supports — an overnight aide, alarms, GPS, day programs — can address the wandering, and documenting the reasoning. Family preference does not displace the least-restrictive analysis, so placing him now on family consensus skips the required step. Petitioning for a secured-perimeter facility is premature until less restrictive alternatives have been shown inadequate.

question: A conservator wants to move a conservatee with advanced Alzheimer's disease into a memory care unit that has a locked perimeter. The conservatee has not been previously placed in a locked setting. What must the conservator establish before this placement can be approved?
options: That the family agrees to the placement and the chosen facility currently has an open bed available
That the conservatee has been hospitalized at some point during the previous thirty calendar days
That she has dementia, cannot consent, would benefit, and that this is the least restrictive setting
explanation: California law (Probate Code §2356.5) requires specific findings before a conservatee may be placed in a secured-perimeter residential care facility: a dementia diagnosis, lack of capacity to give or refuse consent to the placement, that the placement is needed for and would benefit the conservatee, and that it is the least restrictive option. Family agreement and bed availability are practical logistics but are not among the required findings. A recent hospitalization is likewise irrelevant to the four-part test; this is a separate authority that must be specifically requested from the court.

question: Which of the following is an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living (IADL) rather than a basic Activity of Daily Living (ADL)?
options: Bathing oneself and maintaining basic personal hygiene each day
Transferring safely from a bed to a chair without falling
Managing finances and paying monthly household bills on time
explanation: ADLs are basic self-care tasks — bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, transferring, and continence — so both bathing and transferring fall on the ADL side of the line. IADLs are the more complex tasks needed for independent community living: managing finances, shopping, cooking, housekeeping, transportation, and medications. Managing finances and paying bills is the IADL here. The distinction guides needs assessments, since someone who can do ADLs but not IADLs may remain home with limited supports.

question: A conservator suspects a long-term care facility is over-medicating a conservatee with antipsychotics to control behavior. The conservatee is in a Medicare/Medi-Cal certified skilled nursing facility. The administrator dismisses the conservator's concerns. Which of the following is the most appropriate next resource to engage?
options: Adult Protective Services, treating the over-medication strictly as a financial exploitation matter
The local Long-Term Care Ombudsman, the designated advocate for residents of licensed facilities
The District Attorney's office, asking it to open a criminal prosecution of the facility now
explanation: The Long-Term Care Ombudsman, administered by the California Department of Aging, is the designated advocate for residents of long-term care facilities and handles care concerns including chemical restraint and over-medication. Adult Protective Services addresses abuse, neglect, and exploitation, but framing chemical restraint as merely a financial matter misroutes a care-quality concern away from the right specialist. A criminal referral to the District Attorney is premature before the facility-specific advocate has even reviewed the concern.

question: A conservatee with limited mobility wants to remain in her own home. She is enrolled in Medi-Cal and needs help with bathing, meal preparation, and light housekeeping. The conservator is evaluating community resources to support aging in place. Which program is most directly relevant?
options: Regional Center services provided to eligible individuals under the Lanterman Act
Veterans Aid & Attendance, a pension benefit for qualifying wartime veterans
In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS), the Medi-Cal program paying for in-home personal care
explanation: IHSS is the California Medi-Cal program that pays for in-home personal care — housecleaning, meal prep, laundry, shopping, personal care, accompaniment, and protective supervision — for people who would otherwise need facility placement, with a county social worker authorizing hours. Regional Center services are limited to individuals with a qualifying developmental disability, which this conservatee does not have. VA Aid & Attendance is a veterans' pension benefit, not an in-home personal-care program, so neither targets her need the way IHSS does.

question: A 72-year-old conservatee in an RCFE has begun a romantic relationship with another resident. Adult children object and demand the conservator prohibit contact. The conservatee says she is happy and the facility reports no concerns. What is the conservator's best response?
options: Prohibit the contact, since the conservator holds authority over the conservatee's personal life
Move to have her declared unable to consent to any relationship, quietly ending the matter for good
Recognize relationship rights are retained; absent harm or incapacity, respect her autonomy and the staff
explanation: Conservatees retain the right to marry unless the judge specifically removes it, and they retain protected rights to interpersonal and sexual relationships; capacity to consent to intimacy is presumed and is decision-specific. Family objection alone is not a basis to restrict these retained rights, so prohibiting contact overstates the conservator's authority. Seeking to have her declared unable to consent strips rights without evidence of harm or due process; the conservator's role is to monitor for actual harm such as exploitation, not to enforce family preferences.

subtopic: Change of Residence Out of State
question: A conservatee's daughter wants her mother (the conservatee) to move to Texas to live with her permanently. The conservatee is enthusiastic about the idea. The conservator's letters grant only standard authority over the conservatee's residence. What should the conservator do?
options: Petition the court before moving the residence out of state, addressing the plan and her wishes
Approve the move as a routine personal management decision needing no court involvement at all
Deny the move outright, since a conservatee can never relocate away from the State of California
explanation: A probate conservator's authority to fix the conservatee's residence extends only within California, so an out-of-state move requires prior court permission; the petition should address the living arrangements, health care coverage, continued oversight, and the conservatee's wishes, which here favor the move. Approving the relocation unilaterally exceeds the conservator's geographic authority. Denying it outright as categorically forbidden is also wrong — relocation is permitted with court approval, and a flat refusal ignores the conservatee's clearly expressed preference.

question: A conservatee with early-stage dementia continues to drive. The conservator has observed two near-miss incidents and a physician has noted concerns about cognition. The conservatee insists on keeping his license. What is the conservator's most appropriate course of action?
options: Take no action, since driving is a right the conservatee retains and insists on exercising
Refer him for DMV reexamination, arrange transportation alternatives, discuss safety, and document
Take his keys without notice and sell the vehicle so that he is no longer able to drive at all
explanation: The conservator must balance the conservatee's safety with autonomy and dignity. The DMV reexamination process lets physicians, conservators, and others refer a driver for testing, after which DMV may suspend or revoke based on its own assessment; the conservator should also offer transportation, communicate respectfully, document concerns, and seek court guidance if needed. Taking no action exposes the conservatee and the public to harm, while seizing keys and disposing of the car without process disregards his dignity and may not even stop him from driving.

question: A newly appointed probate conservator of the person in California must file a written Determination of Conservatee's Appropriate Level of Care within how many days of appointment?
options: 30 days
90 days
60 days
explanation: California requires the conservator of the person to file a written Determination of Appropriate Level of Care within 60 days of appointment. The 30-day figure is simply too short and matches no required filing here. The 90-day figure is a common distractor because it is the deadline for the conservator of the estate's Inventory & Appraisal, not the level-of-care determination. The determination must address the conservatee's current care level, steps needed to keep them in their residence, and reasons they cannot return if placed elsewhere.

question: A conservatee is being moved from her home into an assisted living facility that does not allow large dogs. She has lived with her elderly Labrador for ten years and is deeply attached. What is the conservator's best approach?
options: Seek pet-friendly housing or family placement with visits, involving her in the decision
Surrender the dog to the local animal shelter right away so the move can be simplified
Let the family decide what happens to the dog without consulting the conservatee about it
explanation: Quality of life and emotional well-being are core duties of the conservator of the person, and a long-bonded companion animal matters greatly during a transition. The conservator should consider pet-friendly housing, placement with a family member or friend who allows visits, or fostering, and involve the conservatee as fully as possible. Surrendering the dog immediately to ease logistics disregards her preferences and well-being, and letting the family decide without consulting her bypasses both the conservator's responsibility and the conservatee's voice.

question: A conservatee is a devout Muslim who prays five times daily, fasts during Ramadan, and follows halal dietary practices. The conservator is selecting a residential care facility. What is the most appropriate way to evaluate options?
options: Choose the lowest-cost licensed facility, regardless of whether it can accommodate religious practice
Identify facilities that provide halal meals, prayer space, and fasting; include her in tours and document it
Address religious practice only later, and only if the conservatee actually complains after she is placed
explanation: Conservatees retain the right to religious expression, and respecting cultural and religious practices is both an ethical duty and part of competent care planning. The conservator should proactively assess whether facilities can accommodate dietary requirements, prayer schedules, and observances, include the conservatee in tours, and document the plan. Selecting purely on cost ignores her retained religious rights and dignity, and waiting for her to complain after placement reacts to a harm the conservator had an affirmative duty to prevent.

question: A conservatee in a skilled nursing facility wants to see her estranged son. Another sibling, who is close to the conservatee, demands the conservator bar the son from visits, alleging he previously took money from the conservatee. The conservatee insists she wants the son to visit. What should the conservator do?
options: Bar the son from visiting immediately, relying on the sibling's allegation that he took money
Allow the son completely unrestricted access without putting any protective safeguards in place
Investigate the financial concerns, consult counsel, and consider supervised or structured visits
explanation: Conservatees retain rights to personal relationships and visitors, and a conservator's authority to restrict visitors is limited, typically requiring evidence of harm and sometimes court involvement. The conservator should investigate the financial allegations, balance protection against the conservatee's expressed wish to see her son, and consider structured options such as supervised visits or financial safeguards before any restriction. Barring the son on an unverified allegation, or allowing unrestricted access despite credible concerns, both skip that balancing and fail the conservator's duties.

question: Where should a conservator look first to determine a conservatee's preferences regarding burial, cremation, or funeral arrangements?
options: The conservatee's own written instructions, then known religious practice and prior statements
Whatever the closest available family member happens to say at the time of the death
The least expensive arrangement available, in order to preserve the value of the estate
explanation: The conservator should look first to the conservatee's documented preferences, which may appear in a will, advance health care directive, prepaid funeral or burial contract, or other writing; where none exists, rely on known religious practice, cultural traditions, and prior statements as substituted judgment. A family member's say-so at the time of death may be considered but cannot override documented wishes. Cost minimization is never the governing standard, since the goal is to honor the conservatee's own preferences, not to economize.

question: A conservator is developing an emergency response plan for a conservatee who lives alone in a single-family home in a wildfire-prone area. Which combination best reflects good emergency planning?
options: Wait until an official evacuation order is finally issued for the area, then react and move quickly
A medical alert device, contact list, evacuation site, ready medications, and transportation plans
Rely on the nearby neighbors to notice and assist the conservatee in the event of any emergency
explanation: Good emergency planning for a vulnerable conservatee is proactive: a medical alert device for in-home emergencies, an emergency contact list, an identified evacuation site, ready access to medications and documents, and transportation and pet-care arrangements made in advance. Waiting for an evacuation order can be too late for someone with limited mobility or cognitive decline, and relying on neighbors without a plan leaves safety to chance. Documenting the plan also satisfies the conservator's duty to anticipate threats to well-being.

question: Which statement best describes the relationship between an Advance Health Care Directive (AHCD) and a Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST) form in California?
options: An AHCD and a POLST are essentially the same instrument, operating under two different names in California
An AHCD is a legal document by which a capable adult appoints an agent and states preferences; a POLST is a provider-signed order
Both are medical orders signed by a physician, the difference being that only a POLST can be used to appoint a healthcare agent
explanation: The AHCD is a legal advance directive completed by an adult with capacity; it appoints a healthcare agent (DPAHC component) and may set out treatment preferences (living will component). The POLST is a portable medical order signed by a physician or other authorized provider that translates wishes into actionable directives like full treatment, limited interventions, or comfort-focused care, and travels with seriously ill or frail patients across care settings. Treating the two as identical ignores that one is a patient-executed legal document and the other a provider order. The claim that both are physician orders is also wrong, and it reverses reality on agents: the AHCD names the agent, while the POLST does not.

question: Which statement best describes the legal standard for a conservatee's capacity to consent to medical treatment?
options: Capacity is presumed and assessed decision-by-decision, turning on understanding the nature, risks, benefits, and alternatives
Capacity is global: once a conservatorship is established the conservatee can no longer consent to any medical decision
Capacity for medical consent may be determined only by a psychiatrist, whatever the particular decision happens to be
explanation: Capacity for medical consent is decision-specific and presumed unless and until a court or qualified evaluator concludes otherwise for a particular decision. Even a person under conservatorship may retain capacity to consent to or refuse some treatments while lacking it for others; the standard is the ability to understand the nature, risks, benefits, and alternatives and to communicate a choice. The 'global' view is wrong because conservatorship does not automatically strip all medical decision-making capacity. The psychiatrist-only view is also wrong: capacity is typically assessed by the treating physician, with specialty input appropriate in some cases but not required for every decision.

question: A physician proposes a hysterectomy for a 30-year-old conservatee with a developmental disability, citing the conservator's preference to prevent pregnancy. The procedure would also resolve recurrent menorrhagia. The conservator believes this is the right course. What is the legal limitation the conservator must recognize?
options: If the physician recommends the procedure, the conservator may consent to it like any other treatment, with no special process
Sterilization, whether the primary or an incidental purpose, requires a separate court order; a conservator cannot consent to it
Consent rests with the conservatee's parent, who retains authority over sterilization regardless of the conservatorship
explanation: A conservator cannot consent to sterilization on behalf of a conservatee. Sterilization — and procedures whose primary or substantial effect would be sterilization, such as a hysterectomy with no medical alternative — is reserved for the court, with heightened procedural protections, especially for persons with developmental disabilities under California law (Probate Code §1958 and related Welfare & Institutions Code provisions). Physician recommendation alone is insufficient, so treating it as routine consent is wrong. A parent has no special authority over an adult conservatee, so deferring to the parent is also wrong. If the menorrhagia can be treated by less drastic means, those should be exhausted first.

question: A conservatee with terminal cancer and full medical decision-making capacity asks her conservator to help her access California's End of Life Option Act (Medical Aid in Dying). The conservator is sympathetic. Which statement best describes the conservator's role?
options: The conservator may sign the aid-in-dying request on the conservatee's behalf because she has asked for the help
Only the patient may request and self-administer, and must have capacity; the conservator cannot consent but may support her access
Aid in dying is unavailable to anyone under a conservatorship, so the conservator cannot lawfully assist with the request
explanation: Under California's End of Life Option Act, the qualifying individual must have capacity, make the request personally rather than through a surrogate, and self-administer the aid-in-dying drug. A conservator cannot consent to it on the conservatee's behalf, so signing for her is not permitted. Conservatorship does not automatically disqualify a person, so the claim that aid in dying is categorically unavailable is also wrong — the conservatee must simply satisfy the capacity and procedural requirements herself. The conservator's role is supportive and informational where appropriate, not substitutive.

question: A person experiencing a psychiatric crisis and meeting criteria for danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability due to a mental disorder can be involuntarily detained for evaluation under California's Lanterman-Petris-Short Act (a '5150 hold') for up to how long?
options: 24 hours
72 hours
14 days
explanation: A 5150 hold authorizes up to 72 hours of involuntary psychiatric detention for evaluation and treatment when a person, due to a mental health disorder, is a danger to self, danger to others, or gravely disabled. The 14-day figure is the next step — a 5250 certification for additional intensive treatment if continued involuntary care is needed — not the initial hold, and 24 hours understates the period. Further holds and LPS conservatorship proceedings require additional process. Memorizing the 72-hour and 14-day intervals is exam-critical.

question: A probate conservatee with dementia is becoming agitated, and the treating physician recommends starting an antipsychotic medication. The conservator has standard authority over personal care decisions but no special grant of medical authority. The conservatee resists. What is the most accurate statement about the conservator's authority here?
options: The conservatee's objection automatically bars administration of the antipsychotic in every case, so the conservator can take no further steps
Psychotropics carry special California protections, sometimes court approval over objection, so the conservator must confirm authority before consenting
Only an LPS conservator may ever consent to any psychiatric medication at all, so a probate conservator has no role whatever in this decision
explanation: A probate conservator with general medical authority can consent to many medications for a conservatee who lacks capacity, but psychotropic medication carries special protections in California, particularly when the conservatee objects — additional court findings (lack of capacity to consent and medical appropriateness) may be required, and forcible administration over objection is constrained. Treating the objection as an absolute bar overstates the conservatee's position and ignores those pathways. The LPS-only view is also wrong: LPS conservators have separate, broader authority, but probate conservators are not excluded from psychiatric medication decisions. The conservator should confirm the scope of authority, document medical necessity, consider least-restrictive alternatives first, and seek counsel and court authority as needed.

question: A conservator of the person is asked by a hospital physician to sign a DNR (Do Not Resuscitate) order for an 88-year-old conservatee in advanced congestive heart failure. The conservatee has no advance directive and no exclusive medical authority has been granted to the conservator. What is the conservator's most appropriate response?
options: Sign the DNR promptly so the order is in place, since a conservator of the person is the one who makes the medical decisions
Engage the team in shared decision-making, gather evidence of prior wishes, assess capacity, and seek court guidance as authority is uncertain
Defer to whichever adult child appears at the hospital first, since the conservatee's close family knows him and his wishes best of all
explanation: DNR decisions are weighty, and a conservator's unilateral authority depends on the scope of the appointment. Without exclusive medical authority or a clear advance directive, the conservator may not be able to authorize a DNR alone, so signing promptly oversteps. Deferring to whichever family member arrives first hands the decision to someone with no legal authority. The proper approach combines assessing the conservatee's capacity for this specific decision (capacity is decision-specific and presumed), gathering substituted-judgment evidence, engaging the team in shared decision-making, and consulting counsel and the court when authority is uncertain.

question: A conservatee with end-stage COPD has a prognosis of less than six months. The conservatee, who has decisional capacity for this issue, says she wants to focus on comfort rather than aggressive interventions. The conservator's adult-child co-conservator wants to continue full curative measures. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Follow the co-conservator's preference for full curative measures, since the two appointed conservators are required to act jointly
Honor her preferences since she has capacity, engage the hospice team, document her goals, and address the disagreement by discussion or court
Consent to hospice only after a formal court hearing is held, regardless of the conservatee's own capacity for this particular decision
explanation: Capacity is decision-specific. A conservatee who has capacity to weigh aggressive treatment against hospice may make that choice for herself, and the conservator's role is to support and advocate, not override — so following the co-conservator's contrary preference disregards the conservatee's own valid choice. Requiring a court hearing despite her capacity adds an unnecessary obstacle, since a court hearing is not required when the conservatee herself can consent. The conservator should engage the hospice team, document goals of care, and resolve the co-conservator disagreement through dialogue, mediation, or court guidance.

question: A researcher invites a conservatee with early-stage Alzheimer's disease to participate in a clinical trial of an experimental drug. The conservator believes participation could benefit the conservatee and other patients. What authority does the conservator have to enroll the conservatee?
options: The conservator may sign the research consent form on the conservatee's behalf, since enrollment in the trial could benefit her
Enrolling a conservatee in experimental research needs court authorization; assess her capacity to assent and never override an objection
Only the IRB chair can approve a conservatee's participation, so the conservator has no role at all once the IRB has acted on the protocol
explanation: Conservatees have a right not to be involved in research projects or drug trials without an additional court order, so the conservator cannot unilaterally sign the consent form even where the trial seems beneficial. The conservator should also assess whether the conservatee has capacity to assent or dissent for this decision; an objection from a conservatee with relevant capacity must be respected. The IRB approves the study protocol generally — it does not substitute for the individual consent and court-authority requirements, so deferring entirely to the IRB chair misunderstands its role. Research is not categorically prohibited, but these safeguards exist because of conservatees' vulnerability.

question: Which statement most accurately describes a probate conservator of the person's access to a conservatee's protected health information under HIPAA?
options: HIPAA blocks all access to a conservatee's protected medical information by anyone other than the conservatee herself
As legal surrogate for a conservatee who lacks healthcare capacity, the conservator is generally a HIPAA personal representative for the information
The conservator must obtain a separate court order from the probate court each and every time the conservatee's medical records are sought
explanation: Under HIPAA, a personal representative with legal authority to make healthcare decisions for an individual is treated as the individual to that extent and may access protected health information. A probate conservator of the person typically qualifies for decisions within the scope of the conservatorship and should provide certified Letters when requesting records. The claim that HIPAA blocks all third-party access is wrong, as is the claim that a fresh court order is needed for each record request. Where the conservatee retains capacity for certain decisions or has specific privacy interests, such as psychotherapy notes, the analysis can be more nuanced.

question: A conservatee who has capacity to consent to medical treatment refuses a recommended surgery to remove a malignant tumor. The conservator believes the surgery is in the conservatee's best interest. What is the conservator's most appropriate response?
options: Authorize the recommended surgery over the conservatee's objection, since the conservator is responsible for protecting her best interest
Petition the court to revoke the conservatee's right to refuse this particular treatment so that the recommended cancer surgery can proceed
Confirm capacity, ensure she has clear information on risks and alternatives, explore her reasons, and respect her decision if capacity is intact
explanation: Capacity for medical consent is presumed and decision-specific. A conservatee with capacity to consent to a particular treatment also has capacity to refuse it. The conservator's role is to ensure the conservatee has the information needed for informed consent, explore the reasons for the choice (addressing reversible factors like depression, fear, or misunderstanding), and respect an autonomous, informed refusal even when the conservator disagrees. Authorizing the surgery over her objection overrides a competent decision, and petitioning to strip her right to refuse attacks her autonomy rather than working within it; both are improper where capacity is intact.

question: A conservatee in a persistent vegetative state has no advance directive. The conservator is asked to make decisions about continued life-sustaining treatment. Family members, friends, and prior conversations suggest the conservatee consistently said she would not want to be kept alive by machines if she had no realistic chance of recovery. How should the conservator approach the decision?
options: Apply substituted judgment from the evidence of her prior wishes, document the analysis, consult counsel, and seek court direction
Default to maximum medical intervention, since there is no written advance directive to direct any other course of action
Defer to whichever family member is the most emphatic about what should be done for the conservatee now
explanation: Substituted judgment asks what the person would want if she could speak, based on reliable evidence of prior expressed wishes, values, and beliefs. Even with no written directive, consistent prior statements to family and friends are probative. Because withdrawal of life support is an extraordinary medical circumstance, the conservator should not act unilaterally — court direction is appropriate and protective. Defaulting to maximum intervention ignores her known wishes, and deferring to the most emphatic family member substitutes that person's insistence for the conservatee's own values, violating the surrogate-decision-making framework.

question: What does it mean when a court grants a conservator 'exclusive authority' to make health care decisions under California law?
options: The conservatee loses every remaining medical right of any kind once the exclusive grant is made by the court
Only the conservator may consent to treatment; without the grant, both the conservator and conservatee may decide
The grant is automatic in every conservatorship of the person, so no separate court finding is ever required
explanation: By default, conservatorship of the person does not strip the conservatee of all medical decision-making — both the conservator and the conservatee may consent, and providers may rely on the conservatee's consent in many situations. When the court makes specific findings, typically a lack of capacity to give informed consent, it may grant the conservator 'exclusive' authority, and the conservator should provide updated Letters to hospitals, doctors, and facilities. The grant does not extinguish every conservatee right, so the first statement overreaches, and it is a meaningful, fact-specific step rather than something automatic in every case.

question: A conservator visits a conservatee in a skilled nursing facility and notices the conservatee is unusually sedated, confused, and unsteady. Staff mention a new medication started the previous week. What is the conservator's best immediate action?
options: Wait and see whether the conservatee gradually adjusts to the new medication over the next several weeks at the facility
Direct the facility nursing staff to discontinue the new medication right away, given these new and troubling symptoms
Promptly contact the physician and pharmacist to review the medication and side effects, document it, and request reconciliation
explanation: The conservator has an active medical-advocacy duty — monitor the conservatee's condition, watch for side effects and interactions, and engage clinicians when concerns arise. Promptly contacting the physician and pharmacist, documenting observations, and seeking medication reconciliation is exactly the expected response. Waiting passively could allow harm to escalate while the conservatee is already symptomatic. Directing the facility to discontinue the medication is outside the conservator's clinical role and could itself cause harm; the proper first step is clinical review by the prescribers.

question: A psychiatrist recommends electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) for a probate conservatee with treatment-resistant major depression. The conservator agrees that the conservatee has not responded to other treatments. Can the conservator authorize the ECT?
options: No — ECT has special California protections, including capacity findings and court authorization where the patient cannot consent
Yes — the conservator may authorize the ECT just like any other recommended and medically appropriate medical procedure
Yes, but only on the condition that a close family member also co-signs the consent for the ECT to proceed
explanation: ECT and other convulsive treatments are subject to heightened protections in California — specific consent and capacity findings are required, and where a patient cannot give informed consent, court authorization is generally needed before ECT may be administered. A probate conservator's general medical authority does not extend to ECT without these safeguards, so treating it as a routine procedure is wrong. Family co-signature is not a substitute for the required findings and court process. The conservator should engage counsel and pursue the proper court process if ECT is being considered.

question: A 78-year-old widow has early-stage dementia but currently understands the nature and consequences of her financial decisions. Her daughter asks you, as a licensed professional fiduciary, what could be put in place now to avoid a future conservatorship if her mother's condition worsens. Which option is the LEAST restrictive and most appropriate first step to recommend, assuming the mother has capacity to execute it?
options: Petition now for a limited conservatorship of the estate to avoid later emergency proceedings
Have the mother execute a durable power of attorney and an Advance Health Care Directive now
Apply to the Social Security Administration to make the daughter her representative payee
explanation: Under the least-restrictive-alternative principle and the Handbook for Conservators, conservatorship is a last resort, so a person with present capacity should execute a durable power of attorney for finances and an Advance Health Care Directive, addressing future incapacity without court involvement. A limited conservatorship is wrong because it is reserved for adults with developmental disabilities, not dementia, and is far more restrictive. A representative payee is too narrow, managing only Social Security benefits while leaving the rest of her estate unaddressed.

question: Under the California Professional Fiduciaries Act, when is a person required to be licensed as a professional fiduciary?
options: When acting as guardian or conservator for any single unrelated person for compensation
When holding themselves out to the public as a professional, whatever the client count
When serving 2+ unrelated conservatees or estates, or as trustee/agent for 3+ individuals
explanation: The Professional Fiduciaries Act (Bus. & Prof. Code §§6500–6592) defines a professional fiduciary by client-count thresholds: guardian or conservator for two or more unrelated persons, personal representative for two or more unrelated estates, or trustee or agent under a power of attorney for three or more individuals. Serving a single unrelated client for pay is below the threshold and typically does not require licensure. Self-described status is irrelevant—licensing is triggered by the client-count thresholds, not by how one markets oneself.

question: You are a professional fiduciary serving as trustee of a trust whose primary income beneficiary is an elderly woman and whose remainder beneficiaries are her three adult children. The income beneficiary needs an expensive in-home caregiver, and one of the remainder beneficiaries objects, arguing the trust should preserve principal for the remaindermen. How should you proceed?
options: Defer to the remainder beneficiary's objection, since the children will outlive the income beneficiary
Split the requested distribution evenly among all four beneficiaries to avoid any favoritism
Apply the trust's distribution standard for the income beneficiary, document it, and seek court instructions if needed
explanation: Under NGA Standards and trust law, the trustee owes loyalty to the beneficiaries as defined by the trust instrument; when the trust authorizes distributions for the income beneficiary's health, maintenance, and support (a HEMS-type standard), the trustee must apply that standard, document the reasoning, and seek court instructions if the dispute escalates. Deferring to the remainderman's objection improperly favors future beneficiaries over a current one in need. Splitting the distribution evenly ignores the trust terms, which direct support to the income beneficiary rather than equal shares.

question: As conservator of the estate, you need to hire a bookkeeper to assist with record-keeping for a complex conservatorship. Your adult son is a competent bookkeeper and offers to do the work at market rate. What is the appropriate course of action?
options: Hire your son, since his rate is competitive and you can directly supervise his work
Hire your son and reduce your own fiduciary fees by his pay to offset the conflict
Avoid hiring your son if reasonable alternatives exist; otherwise disclose and get court approval
explanation: The Handbook for Conservators prohibits hiring family members for paid services when other reasonable alternatives exist; only if no reasonable independent alternative exists may the fiduciary proceed, and then only after full disclosure to the court, a showing that the terms serve the conservatee's best interest, and court approval. Hiring your son because his rate is competitive and you can supervise him is self-dealing absent that process. Reducing your own fees to offset his pay does not cure the disclosure and court-approval requirements that the conflict triggers.

question: In preparing a fee petition, you billed 8 hours at your professional hourly rate for delivering household items to a charity thrift store after the conservatee transitioned to a memory care facility. The court examiner flags this entry. What is the most likely basis for the objection under the three-part reasonableness test?
options: The activity was unnecessary because it provided no benefit to the conservatee at all
The donation needed prior substituted-judgment court approval that was never obtained
The rate was unreasonable for the skill required; a lower-cost worker should have done it
explanation: The three-part reasonableness test asks whether the activity was necessary, whether the rate was reasonable, and whether different rates were used appropriately for different skill levels. Delivering donations is a necessary task but does not require a licensed fiduciary's skill, so billing it at the professional rate fails the skill-level prong. The claim that the activity was unnecessary is wrong, since clearing personal property after placement is part of managing the estate. The claim that substituted-judgment approval was required misapplies that rule, which governs gifts of estate property, not disposing of used household goods after a move.

question: A close friend of your conservatee calls you and asks where the conservatee has been placed and how she is doing. The conservatee has previously told you she does not want this friend to know her whereabouts. There is no evidence of abuse, neglect, or exploitation. What is the appropriate response?
options: Provide the placement address, since a close friend has a legitimate interest in her welfare
Share only the city and her general condition, but withhold the facility's name
Decline to share, while staying polite and offering to relay a message to the conservatee
explanation: Under the NGA Standards and CGC 1.4 (Confidentiality), the fiduciary protects the conservatee's information, guided by whether she would want it disclosed; she has expressed a clear preference and no abuse, neglect, or exploitation exception applies, so the fiduciary should decline while remaining courteous and offering to relay a message. Giving the friend the placement address ignores her stated wishes. Sharing the city and general condition is a partial disclosure that still overrides her autonomy and contradicts her clear instruction.

question: Which type of insurance is generally considered essential for a professional fiduciary practice to manage liability risk?
options: Title insurance covering the conservatee's real property holdings
Long-term care insurance covering the conservatee's future care
Professional liability (E&O) insurance, plus workers' comp if staff are employed
explanation: Risk management for fiduciaries centers on professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance to cover claims of negligence or breach of duty, plus workers' compensation, which is mandatory in California if the fiduciary employs staff. Title insurance is wrong because it pertains to specific real property transactions rather than the fiduciary's practice liability. Long-term care insurance is wrong because it is a personal product for an individual's care costs, not coverage for professional malpractice exposure.

question: You are appointed as co-conservator of the estate with the conservatee's adult son. The son wants to lease a piece of the conservatee's real property to his own business at below-market rent. You believe this is not in the conservatee's best interest. The son insists he has 50 percent decision-making authority. What should you do?
options: Defer to the son's preference, since co-conservators must reach consensus and he is family
Sign the lease but record your disagreement with the terms in your own file
Refuse to sign, document the dispute, and petition the court; the below-market lease is self-dealing
explanation: Co-fiduciaries share duties and cannot ratify a self-dealing transaction; leasing estate property to a co-fiduciary's own business at below-market rent is a textbook conflict under NGA Standards and Probate Code duties, so the remedy is to refuse, document, and petition the court for instructions. Deferring to the son because he is family wrongly treats his 50 percent stake as authority to push through a conflicted deal. Signing under protest while noting disagreement still completes the breach and exposes you to personal liability.

question: You are about to accept a new conservatorship case. During intake you learn that your spouse's small accounting firm has done tax work for the proposed conservatee's son, who is the petitioner. What is the best course of action?
options: Accept without disclosure, since the prior tax work was for the son, not the conservatee
Accept the case but require your spouse's firm to stop all work for the family
Disclose the relationship in writing, and decline if the conflict cannot be cured
explanation: A professional fiduciary must screen for personal, direct, and indirect conflicts before accepting a case; an indirect conflict can arise when a professional connected to the fiduciary—here the spouse's firm—has a relationship with a party tied to the conservatee, so the rule is to disclose in writing and decline if the conflict cannot be managed. Accepting without disclosure because the tax work was for the son overlooks that the son is the petitioner and the link still requires disclosure. Quietly halting the firm's work is a unilateral fix that does not satisfy the disclosure obligation owed to the court and petitioner.

question: When billing time for your fiduciary services, which practice best supports court approval of your fee petition?
options: Lump-sum monthly entries describing the work simply as 'fiduciary services rendered'
Reconstructing the entries each quarter from memory and saved email threads
Contemporaneous entries giving the task, date, time, staff, and skill-appropriate rate
explanation: Court approval of fees requires invoices showing the billable activity, the hours, and the person performing the work, so contemporaneous, task-level entries with skill-appropriate rates meet the three-part reasonableness test and protect the fiduciary if the petition is challenged. Lump-sum entries reading 'fiduciary services rendered' give the court no task-level detail and are routinely reduced or denied. Quarterly reconstruction from memory and emails is unreliable and far weaker than contemporaneous records, drawing the same skepticism on review.

question: During a routine visit to your 82-year-old conservatee in her board-and-care, you observe unexplained bruising on her forearms and notice she has lost weight. A caregiver dismisses your concerns and asks you not to 'stir up trouble.' What is your obligation?
options: Wait until your next monthly visit to see whether the bruising resolves on its own
Discuss it only with the facility administrator and accept their explanation
Document it, report the suspected abuse to APS promptly, and keep the conservatee safe meanwhile
explanation: Professional fiduciaries are mandated reporters under California's Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act, so reasonable suspicion of physical abuse or neglect must be reported to Adult Protective Services (and law enforcement for physical abuse) within the statutory timeframe, with interim steps to keep the conservatee safe. Waiting until the next monthly visit delays a mandated report and leaves her at risk. Discussing it only with the administrator and accepting their explanation substitutes the facility's word for the independent report the law requires.

question: Continuing education for California licensed professional fiduciaries is required because:
options: It is optional but encouraged by PFAC as a professional best practice
It is required only for the initial license, not for each later renewal
Ongoing competence is a regulatory requirement, with set CE hours each license cycle
explanation: Continuing education is mandated by the Professional Fiduciaries Act and Bureau regulations, requiring set CE hours each license cycle because maintaining competence in evolving law and ethics is part of the duty of care owed to clients. Treating it as merely PFAC-encouraged is wrong, because completion is a regulatory requirement, not optional, even though PFAC offers qualifying coursework. Limiting it to the initial license is wrong, since CE applies regardless of caseload and is a condition of every renewal.

question: You are the trustee of a complex special needs trust that holds a concentrated stock position. You delegate investment management to a licensed investment advisor. Two years later, the position has lost substantial value and a beneficiary alleges you breached your duty as trustee. Which of the following best describes your duty when delegating?
options: Delegating to a qualified advisor fully absolves the trustee of investment-related liability
A trustee is not permitted to delegate investment decisions to an outside advisor at all
The trustee must select with care, set the delegation's scope, and monitor performance periodically
explanation: Under the Uniform Prudent Investor Act as adopted in California and NGA Standards, a trustee may delegate investment functions but must select the agent with reasonable care, set a scope consistent with the trust's purposes, and review the agent's performance periodically; delegation does not eliminate this oversight duty, and failure to monitor is itself a breach. The claim that delegation fully absolves the trustee is wrong, because oversight responsibility remains. The claim that delegation is not permitted at all is also wrong, since it is allowed and is often prudent for complex portfolios.

question: The term 'ethnocentrism' as used in fiduciary practice refers to:
options: Adapting one's communication to a client's primary language
Recognizing one's implicit bias and training to overcome it
Judging other cultures by one's own as the standard
explanation: Ethnocentrism is the tendency to judge other cultures as inferior to one's own and to treat one's own cultural norms as the universal standard. It is not the same as adapting communication to a client's language, which is a culturally responsive practice, nor the same as implicit bias, which refers to unconscious attitudes everyone carries rather than an explicit ranking of cultures. Recognizing and counteracting ethnocentrism is foundational to culturally competent fiduciary practice.

question: Your conservatee belongs to a religious tradition that relies primarily on prayer for healing and historically refuses most medical interventions. She is now in early-stage congestive heart failure, and her cardiologist recommends medication that would significantly improve her quality of life. The conservatee, when lucid, says she would prefer prayer alone. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Document her beliefs, consult counsel and her faith community, and seek court guidance if needed
Override her religious preference and authorize the recommended cardiac medication right away
Defer entirely to the cardiologist's recommendation, on the view that providers know best
explanation: When a conservatee relies on prayer alone for healing, those beliefs must be respected, but the conservator must also consult counsel about balancing religious preferences against health-care duties. Overriding her preference and authorizing medication immediately disregards the religious autonomy the Handbook for Conservators directs the fiduciary to honor. Deferring entirely to the cardiologist rubber-stamps the medical view and abandons the balancing duty in the other direction. The best step documents her preference, gathers information from her faith community, an ethics consult, and counsel, and seeks court guidance where conservator authority and religious autonomy genuinely collide.

question: Which of the following best describes the legal definition of a 'developmental disability' as it applies to limited conservatorships in California?
options: Any significant cognitive impairment that is first diagnosed after the age of 65
A severe, chronic disability arising before age 22 with broad functional limits
Any psychiatric diagnosis that is listed in the current DSM-5 classification
explanation: A developmental disability, as used for limited conservatorships, is a severe, chronic disability that originates before age 22, is likely to continue indefinitely, and produces substantial functional limitations in three or more major life activities such as self-care, language, learning, mobility, self-direction, independent living, and economic self-sufficiency. A cognitive impairment first appearing after age 65 describes late-onset dementia, which falls outside the definition. A DSM-5 psychiatric diagnosis alone does not qualify either, since the developmental-disability category turns on early onset and broad functional limitation rather than a mental-health label.

question: Your 72-year-old conservatee has moderate Alzheimer's disease and insists that she is fine, drives just as well as she always has, and does not need any 'help.' Her ability to recognize her own cognitive deficits is markedly impaired. What concept best describes this presentation?
options: Confabulation, the unintentional production of false memories to fill gaps
Malingering, the deliberate faking of symptoms for some external gain
Anosognosia, a neurologically based lack of awareness of one's own deficit
explanation: Anosognosia is the neurologically based inability to recognize one's own cognitive or functional deficit, common in dementia, stroke, and traumatic brain injury, and distinct from ordinary denial — which is why she may genuinely not 'see' her impairment. Confabulation does not fit: it is the production of false memories without intent to deceive, an error of memory rather than a lack of awareness of deficit. Malingering is also different, since it is the deliberate faking of symptoms for gain — the opposite of her sincere belief that she is fine. Recognizing anosognosia informs communication, safety planning, and capacity assessment.

question: Under SB 43 (effective January 1, 2024, with statewide implementation by January 1, 2026), the definition of 'gravely disabled' for LPS conservatorship purposes was expanded. Which statement most accurately reflects the current statutory definition?
options: It adds severe substance use disorder and broadens needs to safety and necessary medical care
It still covers only inability to provide food, clothing, or shelter; SB 43 changed only procedure
It now reaches anyone with a substance use disorder, regardless of how severe that disorder is
explanation: SB 43 expanded the 'gravely disabled' definition two ways: it added severe substance use disorder and co-occurring mental health/substance use disorders as qualifying conditions, and it broadened the deprivation criteria beyond food, clothing, or shelter to include personal safety and necessary medical care. Saying the criteria stayed limited to food, clothing, or shelter understates that substantive expansion. Saying it now reaches anyone with a substance use disorder overstates it, since the statute still requires severity, not any use. The accurate statement captures both the added qualifying conditions and the broadened basic-needs criteria, with LPS still petitioned only by the county Public Guardian.

question: You are a licensed professional fiduciary, and a hospital social worker calls you about a patient with severe schizophrenia who is refusing treatment and has no family. The hospital wants to know if you would consider serving as LPS conservator. What is the correct response?
options: Accept the case, on the basis that LPS authority can be granted to any licensed fiduciary
Explain that only the county Public Guardian may petition, and refer to its LPS investigator
File a probate conservatorship petition instead, since it is essentially the same as an LPS
explanation: LPS conservatorships are governed by the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act and can only be petitioned by the county, typically through the Public Guardian/Public Conservator. Accepting the case is wrong because a private professional fiduciary is not appointed to serve as LPS conservator of the person the way a probate conservator is. Filing a probate conservatorship as a substitute is also wrong, since a probate conservatorship would not authorize involuntary psychiatric treatment. The correct response refers the hospital to the county's LPS conservatorship investigator.

question: Your conservatee, who has paranoid delusions, accuses you of stealing his belongings every visit, despite a meticulous inventory and his housekeeper's confirmation that nothing is missing. He has begun calling the police repeatedly. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Stop visiting him in person so as to avoid triggering the repeated theft accusations
Argue with him at each visit until he finally understands that you did not steal anything
Stay calm, document with witnessed inventories, and coordinate with his treatment team
explanation: Paranoid clients may sincerely believe the fiduciary is deceiving them, and the goal is to manage the situation without abandoning the conservatee.
